text.p: Germany's Bundestag lower house of parliament on Friday passed the government's 1997 federal budget, which is aimed at meeting the Maastricht Treaty's deficit goal and qualify Germany for European monetary union.
Deputies voted by 336 to 313 in favour of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's budget, which will cut federal spending by 2.5 percent to 440 billion marks.
The federal deficit will fall to 53.3 billion marks from an expected 73 billion marks this year.
Taken together with states and municipalities, the total budget deficit is on course for 2.5 percent of gross domestic product, below Maastricht's three percent limit, Waigel said.
Waigel's 1997 budget, first presented in July, has gone through a rocky path of borrowing overshoots, coalition rows and emergency spending cuts to cover likely revenue shortfalls.
But the finance minister said that his goal for joining monetary union was intact: "The numbers show that Germany will qualify for monetary union," he told the closing budget debate.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) kept up their attack on Waigel's credibility, saying that after missing borrowing targets this year the same would happen again next year. "None of the country's problems will be resolved by this budget," SPD finance spokeswoman Ingrid Mattaeus-Maier said.
